Abstract:

Starting the 1910s, Bengal witnessed an alternative printing culture of little magazines. Its experiments included, but were not limited to, providing literary space to young writers which nurtured &ldquonew&rdquo voices, experimenting with language and style, and exploring the &ldquotabooed&rdquo space. The little magazines gradually evolved and functioned as a counter site of experiments, discontinuities, and resistance, thereby paving ways of challenging the predominant printing culture of contemporary Bengal. Moreover, these &ldquoadvance guard&rdquo literary platforms promoted marginal voices&mdashparticularly refugees, Dalits, and women&mdashto articulate their resistance towards dominant cultural values and ideologies. This study examines the contribution of Bangla little magazines in reshaping modern literary culture through formal, linguistic, and thematic innovations. It traces their emergence as transgressive platforms through which marginalized voices contested canon formation and institutional authority in Bengal. Further, it analyses select magazines to highlight the editorial and aesthetic strategies that enabled such interventions. Finally, this study explores their contemporary transformations, focusing on adaptations to globalization, digital publishing, and social media, underscoring their continued relevance as dynamic sites of cultural resistance.

Keywords: Little Magazines Print Culture Alternative literature Marginal Voices Counter-culture Twentieth Century Bengal
